text:
IN THE SUPREME
COURT OF BRITISH COLUMBIA

Citation:

Ross v. British Columbia (Public
Safety)
,

2009 BCSC 1811

Date:
20090928

Docket:
S117620

Registry: New Westminster

Between:

David Jonathan Ross

Plaintiff

And:

Minister of Public Safety and
Solicitor General

of British Columbia and Attorney
General of Canada

Defendants

Before: The Honourable Mr. Justice Schultes

Oral Reasons for Judgment

In Chambers

The Plaintiff, David Jonathan Ross:

Appearing
on his own behalf (via telephone)

Counsel for the Defendants:

M.F.
Volk

R.
Makosz (appearing on

September
28, 2009)

Place and Date of Hearing:

New
Westminster, B.C.

August
13, 2009

Place and Date of Judgment:

New
Westminster, B.C.

September
28, 2009

[
1
]

THE COURT:
This
is an application by the defendants to have the statement of claim struck
without leave to amend and the proceedings dismissed, pursuant to Rule 19(24)
of the
Rules of Court
.  I should note that since the hearing of this
application I have received two packages of material from the plaintiff by
regular mail.  The hearing was intended to encompass all of the submissions of
the parties and no provision was made for me to receive further written
submissions, so I have given both of these packages to the trial coordinators
without opening them.

Background

[
2
]

On March 27, 2008 the plaintiff, who acts on his
own behalf, filed a writ of summons and a statement of claim alleging the following:

On or about
November 2003 Hope RCMP and RCMP of Canada and the Federal Government harassed
and tormented me using surveillance technologies that caused mental and
physical damage to my life which continues to this very day.  The mental and
physical harassment using technology has caused massive financial damages to my
landholdings, my ability to earn a living, and substantial permanent damage to
my physical and mental abilities.  I am under the care of several doctors who
try to help me, who try to treat me for conditions that are not within their
medical expertise.  My life has been tampered with by the Hope RCMP and the
Federal Government, causing me to become a mental, physical and emotional
wreck, not able to function like a normal human being.  Section 269.1, cruel
and unusual punishment, is a violation of the
Criminal Code
, and all of
the above is a violation under the Charter of Canada and the Constitution of
the United States, and a
violation of rights in the United Kingdom.

[
3
]

Damages for various kinds of injuries alleged to
have been inflicted on the plaintiff were also sought.

[
4
]

On October 6, 2008, pursuant to an application
from the defendants, Master Donaldson ordered, among other things, that the
defendant provide better particulars of his claim by November 14, 2008, failing
which it was to be struck without further application.

[
5
]

On January 6th of this year Mr. Justice
Williamson made various orders about the conduct of the case, including that
the plaintiff was at liberty to file a better particularized statement of
claim.

[
6
]

On January 29th the plaintiff filed an amended
statement of claim which read as follows:

I, David Jonathan
Ross, was (2:00 a.m.) questioned in December of 2003 at my property at 21457
Haig Station Road, Hope, B.C., by two RCMP officers from Hope or Chilliwack
RCMP office in regards to a tenant of mine living on my property in a rental
trailer and was the subject of a self-inflicted gunshot wound.  My research has
indicated to me, myself, and perhaps other tenants who are under investigation
and subject to surveillance technology tactics that I have identified in my
sworn affidavit dated January 6th, 2009 and submitted to New Westminster
Supreme Court in courtroom number 214 on January 6th, 2009 before the
Honourable Mr. Justice Williamson.  Specifically, my research has indicated to
me, based on symptoms, neurophone, advanced neurophone and subliminal
messaging, as described in my affidavit.  All of these technologies have U.S. patents and Mr. Patrick Flanagan is
the inventor.

[
7
]

On July 8, 2009 the defendants applied for
summary judgment pursuant to Rule 18(6) on the basis that there was no merit to
the plaintiff's claim.  Mr. Justice Williams dismissed the application at
2009
BCSC 930
.  While he found the allegations "outlandish and unlikely,"
he did not accept that the affidavit on which the defendants relied
demonstrated sufficient expertise or knowledge to be able to establish
conclusively that the surveillance techniques in question were not in use by
that police force.

[
8
]

Mr. Justice Williams noted at the conclusion of
his reasons that he was "somewhat struck" that there had not been an
application by the defendants, pursuant to Rule 19(24) "given the state of
the statement of claim."  These comments, as I understand it, form the
basis of the defendants' present application.

[
9
]

I emphasize for the plaintiff's benefit, as he
is self-represented, that Mr. Justice Williams' comments in that decision about
the possible appropriateness of a future Rule 19(24) application are not
determinative of the present application, which I must decide on its own
merits.

The Basis of the Application

[
10
]

The defendants rely on all of the subsections of
Rule 19(24) to support this application.  They argue that the plaintiff's
pleadings:

a)

discloses no reasonable claim;

b)

is unnecessary, scandalous, frivolous or
vexatious;

c)

is embarrassing; and

d)

is otherwise an abuse of the process of the
court.

[
11
]

During the hearing the plaintiff did not respond
to the merits of the defendants' arguments but expressed his outrage at what he
considered their improper efforts to have his claim struck.

[
12
]

I will consider each of the potential grounds
for dismissal in turn.

Rule 19(24)(a): No Reasonable Claim Disclosed

[
13
]

A court may only strike a statement of claim
pursuant to Rule 19(24)(a) when it is "plain and obvious" that the
claim cannot succeed:
Hunt v. Carey Canada Inc.,
[1990] 2 S.C.J. No. 93
at paragraph 33.  In determining whether this test has been met the court must
assume that the facts in the statement of claim are true and that the case for
the plaintiff is taken at its highest:
Canadian Bar Association v. British
Columbia
(2008),
2008 BCCA 92 (CanLII)
, 76 B.C.L.R. (4th) 48 (C.A.).  However, the court is not
required to assume the truth of allegations that are incapable of proof:
Operation
Dismantle v. The Queen
,
[1985] 2 S.C.R. 441 at 455
.

[
14
]

As long as the pleadings disclose a triable
issue, either as it exists or as it may be amended, the issue should go to
trial:
Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform Inc. v. Canadian Jewish Congress
,

1999 CanLII 5860 (BC SC)
, [1999] B.C.J. No. 2160 (S.C.) 34.  A court is obliged to read the statement of
claim as generously as possible and to accommodate any inadequacies in the form
of the allegations which are merely the result of drafting deficiencies:
Operation
Dismantle
, at page 451.  This is particularly important in the case of a
self-represented plaintiff.

[
15
]

Pursuant to Rule 19(27), no evidence is
admissible in an application under Rule 19(24)(a).

[
16
]

These principles reflect the importance of
removing from the trial process those cases that are inevitably doomed to
failure because of fundamental flaws, while allowing all cases that can
possibly be decided on their merits, including weak or unusual ones, to proceed
to trial.

[
17
]

Although an amended statement of claim would
normally replace the original, I will consider both statements of claim here to
see whether any reasonable claim is disclosed, so that the plaintiff's lack of
drafting skill and failure to carry over certain allegations from one statement
of claim to the next is not the deciding factor.

[
18
]

In the previous application the defendants
characterized the plaintiff's claims as potentially falling into one or more of
the following categories: injury to person, trespass, false imprisonment, or
the civil wrong created by Section 1 of the
Privacy Act
.  I think this
accurately captures all of the potential claims.  I have concluded that,
regardless of which of these potential claims is considered, it is plain and
obvious that the plaintiff's action will fail.

[
19
]

Rule 19(1) requires that a pleading
"contain in summary form the material facts on which the party relies, but
not the evidence by which the facts are to be proved."  "Material
fact" is defined in
Delaney & Friends Cartoon Productions Ltd. v.
Radical Entertainment Inc.
, [2005] B.C.J. No. 573,
2005 BCSC 371
at
paragraph
9
as:

... one that is
essential in order to formulate a complete cause of action.  If a material fact
is omitted, a cause of action is not effectively pleaded.

[
20
]

Rule 19(9.1) provides that:

Conclusions of law
may be pleaded only if the material facts supporting them are pleaded.

[
21
]

The critical omission in the original and
amended statements of claim here is that there are no facts provided to link
the technology that is alleged to have been used against the plaintiff to the
damage that is alleged to have been caused to him.  In his original statement
of claim the plaintiff says that he has been "harassed and tormented"
by the surveillance technologies, that he suffered "mental and physical
harassment," and that "his life has been tampered with."  In his
amended statement of claim he describes having been "subject to
surveillance technology tactics."

[
22
]

There are no facts pleaded that describe the
manner in which this "surveillance technology" produces such
effects.  A trial based on evidence led in support of the current facts alleged
by the plaintiff would inevitably result in a dismissal of the claim because of
this omission in the chain of causation.  I think this is so regardless of
whether the claim is based on physical damage or on an interference with a
right to property or personal privacy.  Integral to the success of any of these
claims would be facts in which the actions of the defendants produced the harm
complained of.

[
23
]

I do not see this as a mere technical omission
or drafting error.  The manner in which the alleged harm was caused cannot be
inferred from the material facts that have been provided.  I appreciate that
the plaintiff has made reference in the amended statement of claim to his
affidavit of January 6th of this year which he says describes the "surveillance
technology tactics" that were used against him, but evidence, whether from
an affidavit or otherwise, is not admissible with respect to my consideration
of Rule 19(24)(a), and the statement of claim must stand or fall on the basis
of its contents.

[
24
]

In this regard I would distinguish the
plaintiff's statements of claim from the plaintiff's statement in
Jerry Rose
Jr. v. University of British Columbia
,
2008 BCSC 1661
, an authority relied
on by the defendants.  That statement of claim, while ultimately found to be
defective for other reasons, did include sufficient facts to support the cause
of action.

Rule 19(24)(b): Unnecessary, Scandalous,
Frivolous or Vexatious

[
25
]

A pleading is "unnecessary" if it does
not go to establishing the plaintiff's cause of action, or does not advance any
claim known in law,
Citizens for Foreign Aid Reform
, at paragraph 47.

[
26
]

"Scandalous" is given its ordinary
meaning when used in this context, "An allegation which is scandalous will
not be struck if it is otherwise relevant to the proceedings.  It will only be
struck if it is irrelevant as well as scandalous":
Citizens for Foreign
Aid Reform
, at paragraph 47.

[
27
]

A pleading is frivolous if it is without
substance, is groundless, fanciful, trifles with the court or wastes time:
McNutt
v. A.G. Canada et al
,
2004 BCSC 1113
at paragraph
40
.  A pleading is
vexatious if it is without
bona fides
, is hopelessly oppressive, or
causes the other party anxiety, trouble or expense:
Borsato v. Basra
,

[2001] B.C.J. No. 84 (S.C.)
, reversed on other grounds,
2000 BCSC 1898 (CanLII)
, [2000] B.C.J. No. 2855.

[
28
]

As in the case of the applications under
sub-rule 19(24)(a), the test is whether it is plain and obvious that the action
cannot succeed, based on one or more of these deficiencies.  Subject once again
to the exception for allegations that are incapable of proof, the facts alleged
are assumed to be true for the purpose of this analysis.

[
29
]

With those limitations in mind, I cannot say
that any of the factors under this sub-rule are engaged by the statement of
claim.  As I have said under the previous section, the problem with the
pleadings is the absence of the central material facts to support any causes of
action.  This is not to say that no claim known to law could ever have arisen
from them if the required facts were present and were assumed to be true.  I
cannot therefore say that the pleadings are unnecessary.

[
30
]

Similarly, once one has crossed the Rubicon of
assuming the unusual facts alleged by the plaintiff to be true, there is
nothing further within that context of assumed facts that is additional
fanciful or without foundation, so I would not characterize them as being
frivolous.  The pleadings could potentially be described as scandalous in that
they allege wrongdoing by members of the RCMP, but I am satisfied that this
scandalous aspect is inherent in the claims that are being pleaded.  If those
claims had been supported by material facts, any scandalous effect would be
excused on the basis of relevance.

[
31
]

THE PLAINTIFF:  Your Lordship --

[
32
]

THE COURT:  Please wait until I finish my
judgment.

[
33
]

Finally, I am unable to ascribe any improper
purpose or lack of good faith to the plaintiff so as to make the pleadings
vexatious.  This action has likely been inconvenient and costly to defend, but
it cannot fairly be described as being oppressive to the defendants.

Rule 19(24)(c): Prejudice, Embarrass
or Delay

[
34
]

A pleading is embarrassing if it does not state
the real issue in intelligible form.  It is also embarrassing if it is prolix,
includes irrelevant facts, arguments or evidence.  It is prejudicial if it is
constructed in a manner calculated to confuse the defendants and make it
difficult, if not impossible to answer,
McNutt
, at paragraph
41
.

[
35
]

I think the plaintiff's statements of claim are
embarrassing in the first sense described above.  For the same reason that they
fail to disclose a reasonable claim, the statements of claim's omissions with
regard to how the surveillance is actually alleged to have harmed the
plaintiff, mean that the real issue has not been stated in an intelligible
form.  It will be impossible for the defendants to plead anything other than a
general denial in response.

[
36
]

I do not view the statements as being
prejudicial in the sense described above.  The confusion that the defendants
will experience in attempting to respond cannot be said to result from any
"calculated construction" of the statements to achieve that purpose.
I do think, however, that the statements of claim would have the effect of
delaying any trial that would be held in that extensive and time-consuming
disclosure and discovery would be needed to identify the actual nature of the
wrongs being alleged.

Abuse
of the Court’s Process

[
37
]

A pleading is an abuse of process if the
litigation process is used for an improper purpose, eg. where the proceedings
constitute a sham, where the process of the court is not being fairly or
honestly used, or is employed for some ulterior or improper purpose:
McNutt
,
at paragraph
42
.  The plaintiff's statement of claim does not meet this
definition.  Whatever their shortcomings, his belief in the allegations that
they contain appears to be genuine.

Conclusions

[
38
]

The statements of claim will be struck out on
the basis that they disclose no reasonable claim and that they will embarrass
and delay any trial based on them.  The absent material facts, if they exist,
are solely within the knowledge of the plaintiff and there is no way for this
court to amend the statements of claim to address their deficiencies.

[
39
]

In any event, given the length of time that this
matter has been outstanding, and the two previous applications in which the
factual sufficiency of the statements of claim has been a central issue, I have
confidence that the deficiencies could be remedied by granting further
opportunities to amend.  One must bear in mind that the plaintiff has not been
asked to produce complex legal material beyond the abilities of a self-represented
litigant, but merely to state those essential facts on which his claim rests.

[
40
]

Accordingly, the proceedings will be dismissed.
Although Rule 19(24) specifically provides that the court may order special
costs in the event of a successful application of this kind, provided that the
criteria for special costs are otherwise met, the defendants very fairly have
not sought such costs against the plaintiff.  I commend the defendants for
their restraint and in that regard I will order

only the usual costs at Scale B against
the plaintiff.

“Schultes J.”
